title: Governance & Accountability
summary: Proving what the system did, for whom, and at what cost. 5 building blocks drilled by recall: the signal that says reach for one, what it costs, how it breaks, which sibling rules it out, and what it is doing across the canonical problems.
keyTakeaways: Audit Log & Provenance — An append-only record of what was decided and what it was shown, pinned to the versions in effect, so the decision can be reconstructed later.
Agent Decision Record — The row an autonomous decision writes about itself: what it chose, why, how sure it was, and what it was looking at when it chose.
Cost Metering — Attributing the marginal cost of a request to the tenant and unit of work that caused it, then bounding it before it is spent.
Progressive Rollout — Earning a change's blast radius in stages, so each widening is justified by evidence the previous stage produced.
Tenant Isolation — Keeping one customer's data and load away from another's, enforced below application code so a forgotten predicate cannot leak.

questions.prompt: You put Audit Log & Provenance in a design. Name the signals that should have stopped you — and what it costs even when it is the right call.
points: The decision is trivially re-derivable from durable inputs you already retain — then the log stores no information you did not have
You only want debugging visibility, where tracing and structured logs are cheaper and are built for the job
The record outlives the schema that wrote it, so it must be self-describing and denormalized rather than a web of foreign keys
Retention is measured in years and is usually a legal floor rather than a tuning knob
Evidence has to be captured at decision time, which means storing the third-party response rather than the query that produced it
Write amplification on every step of every decision, which is the price of the record being complete rather than sampled

questions.prompt: Audit Log & Provenance vs Transactional Outbox / CDC vs Stream Processing — what decides between them?
points: Transactional Outbox / CDC — Captures every state change for downstream consumers; an audit log captures the decision and its justification, which a change feed does not carry.
Stream Processing — When the question is aggregate behaviour over time rather than the defensibility of one specific decision.
Audit Log & Provenance — An append-only record of what was decided and what it was shown, pinned to the versions in effect, so the decision can be reconstructed later.
questions.answer: Transactional Outbox / CDC: Captures every state change for downstream consumers; an audit log captures the decision and its justification, which a change feed does not carry. Stream Processing: When the question is aggregate behaviour over time rather than the defensibility of one specific decision.

questions.prompt: Audit Log & Provenance appears in 6 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.
points: Design a Payment System (Wallet / Ledger) — A double-entry ledger is the audit trail: the balance is derived from immutable entries rather than stored, so any figure can be re-proved from the entries that produced it.

Design an Ad Click Aggregator — Raw events are kept in object storage and a nightly batch recompute is the authority, so the fast streaming number is always reconcilable against a durable record of what actually arrived.

Design a Financial Crime Alert Investigation System — An examiner can ask years later why one alert was cleared, so the trace pins prompt, model snapshot, policy version and evidence hashes — everything whose change would change the answer.
Design a Sanctions Screening System — Every screening decision records the list version it ran against, since 'we did not know' is only defensible with the evidence attached.

Design a Human Review Queue — A reviewer's decision is written as an immutable event with its reason and the lease that authorised it, and a correction references the original rather than overwriting it.
Design a Business Verification Pipeline — Sources disagree routinely, so the record keeps what each one said and which precedence rule decided between them, rather than silently keeping the winner.

questions.prompt: You put Agent Decision Record in a design. Name the signals that should have stopped you — and what it costs even when it is the right call.
points: The decision is a pure function of stored inputs and a rule you version anyway, where re-running the rule is cheaper and more honest than a narration of it

questions.prompt: Agent Decision Record is in your design and load goes up ten times. How does it break?
points: Free-form reason strings instead of a closed enum, which yields thousands of near-duplicates and no dimension to group by
Storing only the applied outcome, so whether a human agreed with the agent cannot be reconstructed and the autonomy metric does not exist
Treating a self-reported rationale as proof of reasoning rather than evidence of it, when the model narrates after the fact and can narrate wrongly
Collapsing confidence in the answer and completeness of the evidence into one score, which hides the dangerous quadrant where the agent is sure and underinformed
Encoding abstention as low confidence plus an escalation, so missing evidence and conflicting sources land in the same bucket and neither gets fixed
Referencing a threshold that lives only in config, so the row cannot say what bar it actually cleared

questions.prompt: Agent Decision Record vs Audit Log & Provenance vs Progressive Rollout — what decides between them?
points: Audit Log & Provenance — The general provenance record for any decision; this is the shape it takes when the decider is a model, adding calibrated confidence, an abstention state and the agree/disagree column.

Progressive Rollout — The mechanism that raises the automated share; this record is the evidence it runs on, because you cannot widen the band without knowing where the agent and the reviewer diverged.
Agent Decision Record — The row an autonomous decision writes about itself: what it chose, why, how sure it was, and what it was looking at when it chose.

Progressive Rollout: The mechanism that raises the automated share; this record is the evidence it runs on, because you cannot widen the band without knowing where the agent and the reviewer diverged.

questions.prompt: Agent Decision Record appears in 3 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.
points: Design a Financial Crime Alert Investigation System — Every auto-closed alert carries the reason code it closed under, the agent's confidence, the threshold in force that day, and whether a reviewer later disagreed.
Design a Human Review Queue — The reviewer's verdict is stored beside the agent's recommendation rather than replacing it, so the disagreement rate is a number instead of an impression.

Design a Business Verification Pipeline — A verification records which source it believed and how sure it was, so an approval on thin evidence is visible rather than indistinguishable from a confident one.

questions.prompt: Cost Metering vs Rate Limiting vs Resource Scheduling vs Load Shedding — what decides between them?
points: Rate Limiting — Bounds request volume; a budget bounds spend, and one expensive request can blow the budget while staying inside the rate limit.
Resource Scheduling — Allocates scarce compute between competing work; metering decides what that work was allowed to cost in the first place.
Load Shedding — Drops work to protect latency; a budget stops work to protect the bill, and they can disagree about which request to drop.
Cost Metering — Attributing the marginal cost of a request to the tenant and unit of work that caused it, then bounding it before it is spent.
questions.answer: Rate Limiting: Bounds request volume; a budget bounds spend, and one expensive request can blow the budget while staying inside the rate limit. Resource Scheduling: Allocates scarce compute between competing work; metering decides what that work was allowed to cost in the first place. Load Shedding: Drops work to protect latency; a budget stops work to protect the bill, and they can disagree about which request to drop.

questions.prompt: Cost Metering appears in 3 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.
points: Design an LLM Inference Platform — GPU seconds are the scarce resource and the KV cache sets how many sequences fit, so admission is a spend decision per request rather than a queueing one.

Design a Financial Crime Alert Investigation System — An agent choosing its own tools is spending money autonomously, so each case carries a hard budget and cost becomes an input to tool selection rather than a report afterwards.

Design a Business Verification Pipeline — A full ownership walk can fire dozens of paid lookups, so checks are ordered by cost and information gain and results are cached per entity across applications.

questions.prompt: Progressive Rollout vs Circuit Breaker vs Bulkhead Isolation — what decides between them?
points: Circuit Breaker — Reacts to a failure that is already happening; a rollout bounds how much traffic could have been exposed to it.
Bulkhead Isolation — Contains blast radius by partitioning resources rather than by limiting how much traffic sees the change.
Progressive Rollout — Earning a change's blast radius in stages, so each widening is justified by evidence the previous stage produced.
questions.answer: Circuit Breaker: Reacts to a failure that is already happening; a rollout bounds how much traffic could have been exposed to it. Bulkhead Isolation: Contains blast radius by partitioning resources rather than by limiting how much traffic sees the change.

questions.prompt: Progressive Rollout appears in 5 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.
points: Design an LLM Inference Platform — New model versions take a slice of traffic before all of it, because quality regressions are only visible against real prompts.
Design a Short-Form Video Feed — A new ranker is exposed to a fraction of the feed first, since offline metrics routinely disagree with what people actually watch.
Design a Feature Store — A changed feature definition rolls out gradually, because training/serving skew surfaces as slow quality drift rather than as an error.
Design a Content Moderation Pipeline — A new moderation model runs in shadow before it can action anything, since a false positive here removes legitimate content.
Design a Financial Crime Alert Investigation System — A new agent version is scored against decisions humans already made before it is trusted to dispose of alerts on its own.

questions.prompt: Tenant Isolation vs Bulkhead Isolation vs Rate Limiting vs Sharding — what decides between them?
points: Bulkhead Isolation — Isolates load between workload classes; tenancy adds a data boundary that a bulkhead says nothing about.
Rate Limiting — Caps a tenant's request rate, which is the load half of isolation and none of the data half.
Sharding — Splitting by tenant makes isolation physical, at the cost of per-tenant operations and rebalancing.

questions.prompt: Tenant Isolation appears in 5 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.
points: Design an LLM Inference Platform — Per-tenant GPU pools and quotas, so one customer's batch job cannot consume the capacity another customer's interactive traffic depends on.
Design an Observability Platform — Per-tenant ingest partitions and query limits, so one customer instrumenting a hot loop cannot degrade everyone else's dashboards.

Design a Financial Crime Alert Investigation System — Each bank's policy, data and model configuration stay separate, because the same agents run against institutions that must never see each other's alerts.
Design a Human Review Queue — Reviewer pools and queues are scoped per tenant, since someone cleared to see one institution's data usually is not cleared for another's.
Design a Business Verification Pipeline — Per-institution verification policy and vendor credentials, so 'sufficient evidence' can mean two different things in the same pipeline.
